goal.text: Build the most correct, most complete Magnetar zkVM in Rust: every component of the paper, sound end to end, at 120 bits, measured against the paper's own tables, and then better.
goal.full:
Drew, 2026-10-17: "use [free GLM 5.3 Flash] to actually build this zkvm out the most correct the most amazing ambitious thing". Build the most correct, most complete Magnetar zkVM in Rust: every component of the paper, sound end to end, at 120 bits, measured against the paper's own tables, and then better.

Drew, 2026-10-16, on Magnetar (Setty, Microsoft Research, ePrint 2026/2423): "can it build in complete rust like the most senior eng team would do https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/research/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/magnetar-1.pdf, implement the paper and prove it, that's the plays goal, we should run for literally as long as we can possibly do it" and "after its built we can hillclimb every metric about it, reduce proof size, reduce proving / verifying time, make it more parallelized, make ASICs and prove they're good, no fake bs, no overuse of mocked tests and unit tests."

Magnetar is the first transparent, hash-based, post-quantum zkVM for the general-purpose RV64I ISA, at 120 bits of provable security, whose security rests on standard hashes (SHA-256 or SHA-3) alone, with no trusted setup, no elliptic curves or lattices, no circuit-friendly hash, and no conjectured Reed-Solomon proximity gap. Build it in Rust from the paper and prove it works: a preprocessor that turns a program into a succinct verifying key, a prover that produces a succinct proof of an RV64I program execution on a given input, and a separate verifier that — holding only the verifying key, not the program — accepts an honest proof and rejects a dishonest one. The paper's parts are BinarySpartan (Spartan over binary fields, ePrint 2026/1656), Virtual Spartan, BinaryTwist and BinaryShout (Twist and Shout over binary fields, with the one-hotness refinement), BinaryRouter (sum-check arguments for bit routings: shifts and sub-word stores), and MosaicPCS over Ligerito (ePrint 2025/1187), with SHA-256 / SHA-3 Fiat-Shamir. No public BinarySpartan or Ligerito implementation was found, so this is a clean-room implementation from the paper; the paper text is mounted as the first source.

The brief is a starting point, not a fence, and it is not exhaustive or self-contained. Own this outcome as the most senior zkVM engineering team would. Reason from first principles about what a correct, sound, succinct implementation of this paper needs; find what the brief leaves out and fill it. The check, its bar, the deliverable and the bounds stay fixed; everything else — the architecture, the module seams, the memory layout, the arithmetization, the parallelism — is yours.

Drew, 2026-10-19: "use the most battle tested and professional libraries … to help" and "the point is one play that does everythign!" Build the way that senior team would. For every primitive a mature, audited, licence-compatible Rust crate already provides, reuse it, vendored so the offline build works. That covers binary tower and GF(2^128) field arithmetic with its SIMD backends (PCLMULQDQ, VPCLMULQDQ, GFNI, AVX-512, NEON/PMULL), SHA-256, SHA-3 and Merkle hashing, Reed-Solomon encoding and additive FFTs, multilinear polynomials, parallelism, and benchmarking. Spend the team on what no library provides: the paper's protocols, their soundness, and their speed. arkworks targets prime fields and elliptic curves, not this paper's binary tower fields, so look for libraries built for binary fields, and check each one's licence and fitness before you adopt it. Name each library choice and the alternatives you rejected in handoff.md. Code you already wrote stays only where it beats the library you measured it against.

Own the whole result, not one part of it: every component of the paper, its soundness at 120 bits, its speed, and its platforms (x86_64 and aarch64). Measure every release yourselves against the paper's Tables 2 and 3 at the paper's scale (2^20 to 2^24 cycles) with a benchmark you build, commit and re-run on every release tag, because the check proves only 4,096-cycle workloads.
